proposals.relationship: Dickason praises Carter’s corrective history of western Canada but argues that it idealizes Indigenous societies and generalizes equality too broadly (2001).
proposals.evidence_note: A bounded criticism within an appreciative review of Aboriginal People and Colonizers of Western Canada to 1900. The substantive review is reproduced in the institutional repository’s abstract field; that primary text was read, but the PDF returned 403 and was not facsimile-collated. Carter’s book body remains unread. Dickason’s separate buffalo example is not needed to substantiate this relationship.
primary_locators: Great Plains Quarterly 21.3 (Summer 2001), p.235; repository transcription, second paragraph beginning with the richer texture of Carter’s history and final appreciative paragraph.

proposals.relationship: Dickason questions Pagden’s account of rejected imperial doctrines by distinguishing theoretical argument from their continued use in practical colonial policy (1997).
proposals.evidence_note: Review of Lords of All the World, especially its treatment of Hostiensis and Edward Coke. She also praises the book’s contribution to comparative colonial studies; this is not rejection of the whole project. The review’s original heading prints Worlds, whereas the identified 1995 book title uses World. Full review read; Pagden’s book body remains unread.
primary_locators: The Canadian Historical Review 78.1 (1997), pp.171–173; p.172 paragraph beginning with critics of empire, and p.173 final appreciative paragraph.

proposals.relationship: Deloria incorporates Dickason’s The Myth of the Savage into his account of critical scholarship on the images and discourses that accompanied conquest, crediting its extension to French contexts (2002).
proposals.evidence_note: A named historiographical resource, not personal mentoring or a comprehensive intellectual lineage. Deloria credits Gordon Sayre alongside Dickason. The particular paragraph on p.10 was freshly read and visually checked; Dickason’s book body remains unread. This claim is distinct from Deloria’s already mapped Turner criticism and Wilson resource.
primary_locators: Philip J. Deloria, “Historiography,” A Companion to American Indian History (2002), p.10, second paragraph.

proposals.relationship: Medicine’s 2003 review identifies Dickason’s historical insights among the Indigenous scholarly resources Carter uses in her history of Aboriginal people and colonizers in western Canada.
proposals.evidence_note: Explicitly attributed to Beatrice Medicine’s substantive review of Carter’s 1999 book, whose body remains unread. Harold Cardinal, Paul Chartrand and Edward Ahenakew retain co-credit. This establishes reported use of historical insight, not mentorship, exclusive influence, or a particular Dickason work. It is distinct from Dickason’s own 2001 criticism of Carter; Medicine’s Big Bear example and Christine Welsh’s formulation are not assigned to Dickason.
primary_locators: Canadian Journal of Native Studies 23.1 (2003), p. 197, paragraph beginning with the ethnohistorical method; author signature and preceding p. 196 checked.
